events.title: Trump signs executive order directing DHS to immediately pay TSA agents during partial shutdown
events.summary: President Trump signed an executive order on Friday, March 28, 2026, instructing the Department of Homeland Security to immediately pay Transportation Security Administration agents who had gone without pay for over 42 days due to a partial government shutdown. The order came after House Republicans rejected a Senate-passed funding deal for key DHS subagencies. Trump blamed Democrats for prioritizing "criminal illegal aliens" over American citizens. DHS confirmed TSA began paying its workforce immediately, with officers potentially receiving paychecks by March 30. The shutdown had caused nationwide staffing shortages, record airport wait times, and nearly 500 TSA resignations.
events.why_relevant: The executive order represents a unilateral presidential action to circumvent stalled congressional negotiations and fund a federal agency during a shutdown, raising questions about executive authority, appropriations power, and the separation of powers.
events.basis: Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday instructing the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to immediately pay Transportation Security Administration agents as the partial shutdown drags on.

events.title: Trump signs presidential memorandum directing DHS to pay TSA employees from available funds
events.summary: Trump signed a presidential memorandum late Friday, March 28, directing DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin to restore pay to TSA employees who had missed two paychecks. The memo instructed the secretary to redirect funds "that have a reasonable and logical nexus to TSA operations" to cover accrued pay and benefits. White House border czar Tom Homan stated the measure was "a start" but acknowledged thousands of other DHS employees remained unpaid and that ICE deployment at airports would continue pending TSA staffing recovery.
events.why_relevant: A presidential memorandum attempting to circumvent congressional appropriations authority raises constitutional questions about separation of powers and the legality of executive fund-redirection during a shutdown.
events.basis: Trump signed a memo late on Friday ordering DHS to restore pay to TSA employees, who have missed two paychecks, but it is unclear where that money will come from and if he can legally direct the agency to pay the employees.

events.summary: The Drug Enforcement Administration finalized a rule designating 2-methyl-3-phenyloxirane-2-carboxylic acid (P2P methyl glycidic acid), its esters, isomers, salts, and related compounds as a List I chemical under the Controlled Substances Act. The designation subjects all handlers—manufacturers, distributors, importers, exporters—to registration, recordkeeping, reporting, security, and inspection requirements. Chemical mixtures containing any amount of P2P methyl glycidic acid are regulated unless exempted by DEA application.

events.summary: The Food and Drug Administration issued a final order classifying the BrainTemp Neonate (BTNeo) System—a brain temperature measurement device—into Class II (special controls) under 21 CFR 882.1565. events.title: Trump's 50% gas price reduction pledge unfulfilled; prices increased 28% instead
events.summary: During his 2024 campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly pledged to reduce gasoline prices by 50% within 12 months of taking office, declaring on October 10, 2024, that gas would cost $1.57 per gallon by January 2026. On January 20, 2025, when Trump took office, gas averaged $3.12 per gallon. As of March 31, 2026, gas prices had risen to $4.02 per gallon—a 28% increase rather than the promised 50% decrease. events.title: US Supreme Court hears oral arguments in Pitchford death penalty case involving alleged racial bias in jury selection
events.summary: The US Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Pitchford v. Mississippi, a capital murder case in which prosecutor Doug Evans removed nearly all Black jurors from the 2006 trial jury that convicted Terry Pitchford. The case centers on whether trial judge Joseph Loper properly applied the Batson v. Kentucky standard prohibiting race-based jury strikes. Conservative justices focused on whether defense counsel should have objected more forcefully, while liberal justices questioned whether the defense waived her argument or was rebuffed by the judge. The case echoes the Court's 2020 reversal of Curtis Flowers' conviction in a similar Evans-prosecuted case.
events.why_relevant: The case directly implicates the constitutional right to a jury free from racial discrimination and tests whether courts adequately enforce protections against prosecutorial race-based jury strikes, a foundational element of equal justice.

However, the court dismissed claims challenging the categorical nature of the terminations as unreviewable. Consequently, the court vacated the April 2025 parole terminations for the certified class and ordered DHS to restore class members to their prior parole status.

events.title: EPA Finalizes National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Chemical Manufacturing Area Sources Technology Review
events.summary: The Environmental Protection Agency finalized amendments to the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) for Chemical Manufacturing Area Source (CMAS) categories, implementing a mandatory technology review under Clean Air Act section 112(d)(6). The final rule establishes new leak detection and repair (LDAR) requirements for equipment leaks and heat exchange systems, adds standards for pressure relief devices and pressure vessels, requires electronic reporting for compliance notifications and performance test results, and mandates continuous performance testing of non-flare air pollution control devices. The rule affects 251 facilities across nine CMAS categories and is estimated to reduce hazardous air pollutant emissions by approximately 160 tons per year. The EPA deferred final action on proposed ethylene oxide (EtO) area source standards pending further consideration and coordination with major source regulations.
events.why_relevant: This final rule expands federal environmental regulatory authority over chemical manufacturing facilities, imposing new monitoring, testing, and reporting obligations that affect industrial operations and compliance costs across multiple states.

events.title: Trump proclamation strengthens metal tariffs, expands scope to full customs value, raises rates to 50 percent for aluminum and steel.
events.summary: President Trump issued Proclamation 11021 on April 2, 2026, modifying tariff regimes on aluminum, steel, and copper imports established under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
